body: Welcome. Over roughly ninety days you will get one short note a day about becoming someone who writes things down, not for an audience, just to think a little more clearly.
Today, find something to write on. Any notebook, the back of an envelope or a notes app will do. Fancy stationery can wait.
Write one sentence about how today went. Only one. Stopping there is allowed, and probably wise.
Notice when your head feels crowded today. That busy, looping feeling is exactly what a page is good at holding for you.
A journal is not a diary for posterity. Think of it as a workbench where half-formed thoughts can be laid out and looked at.
Pick a time that already exists in your day, such as the kettle boiling or the bus home, and attach two minutes of writing to it.
Write down three things on your mind right now, in any order. Seeing them listed often makes them feel smaller.
Handwriting is slower than typing, and that slowness can help. Try a few lines by pen today and see whether it changes anything.
Spelling, grammar and neat handwriting do not matter here. Nobody is marking this. Let the sentences be scruffy.
Keep your notebook somewhere you will see it, not in a drawer. Visible tools get used far more than hidden ones.
Write the date at the top of today's page. That tiny ritual tells your brain a session has started.
If you miss a day, simply write today. There is no backlog to catch up on and no streak to mourn.
Try finishing this sentence: what I keep meaning to think about properly is... Then give it five lines.
Notice how you feel just after writing, compared with just before. Even a small shift in calm is worth noting.
Some people write in the morning to plan, others at night to empty out. Experiment with both this week and see which suits you.
Two weeks in. Flick back through what you have written so far. What surprises you about your own pages?
Today, write about a decision you are weighing. Put the options in two columns and see what jumps out once it is on paper.
When a worry arrives, jot it down with the time. Later, read it back and ask whether it still feels as urgent.
Try a brain dump: set a timer for five minutes and write without lifting the pen. Stop when it rings, wherever you are.
Write about one conversation from today. What was said, and what did you wish you had said?
A page can hold contradictions. You are allowed to write that you want two opposite things at once.
Questions make good prompts. Write one question at the top of the page and let yourself wander towards an answer.
Note one small thing you noticed today that you would otherwise forget: a smell, a phrase overheard, the colour of the sky.
If the blank page feels heavy, begin with what you can see from where you are sitting. Description warms the hand up.
Write about something that irritated you today, then add a line about what that irritation might be pointing to.
Try writing in lists today rather than sentences. Some days your thinking comes out in bullet points, and that is fine.
Keep the entry short on purpose. Three lines written is better than a page you never start.
Write down a plan for tomorrow in three steps. Tomorrow evening, look back and see how close the day came to the plan.
Notice the stories you tell yourself in your entries. Are you the hero, the victim or the narrator? Just observe it.
Write a short letter you will never send to someone who is on your mind. Say plainly what you would like them to know.
A month of notes. Which time of day, place and format seems to work best for you? Write down your current routine as it really is.
Try ending each entry with one line that starts with: what I will do next is. It turns reflection into a small step.
Write about something you are looking forward to. Anticipation is easier to enjoy when you have named it.
On a busy day, a single word summing up your mood still counts. Write the word and the date and close the book.
Write about a mistake you made recently, as plainly as a news report. Facts first, feelings second, lessons last.
Try writing from the point of view of yourself a year from now, looking back on this week. What would that person notice?
When you are stuck on a problem at work or home, write it out as if explaining it to a friend. The gap in your reasoning often appears.
Underline one sentence from this week's pages that feels true. Copy it onto a fresh line where you will find it again.
Write about where your energy went today. Which hours drained you and which filled you back up?
If you notice yourself writing the same complaint again and again, circle it. Repeated lines are clues worth following.
Today, write a list of ten small things you would like more of in your life. Do not judge the list, just make it.
Try a sentence-starter for a quick entry: today I learned, today I noticed, today I avoided. Pick whichever fits.
Keep a pen clipped to your notebook. Hunting for something to write with is one of the quiet ways a habit fades.
Write about a place that matters to you. Describing it in detail is a good way to discover why it stays with you.
If you have been writing only when things go wrong, try writing on an ordinary good day too. Your pages deserve the full picture.
Six weeks in. Read one entry from your first week. How has the way you write, or what you write about, shifted since then?
Some thoughts only make sense on the third attempt. Write the same idea three ways today and see which version sounds most honest.
Write before a hard conversation. Note what you want, what you fear, and the one point you most want to get across.
Write after that conversation too, if it happens. Compare it with what you predicted on the page beforehand.
When you feel overwhelmed, write the next single action you can take, no matter how small. Then go and do just that.
Try writing about a feeling without naming it. Describe where it sits in your body and what it makes you want to do.
Writing can be slower than thinking, which is useful when your mind is racing. Let the pen set the pace today.
When a strong opinion forms, write down the best argument against it. You may not change your mind, but you will understand it better.
Before sleep, jot down anything still buzzing in your head. Parking it on paper tells your mind it can stop holding it overnight.
Write about a habit you are trying to change. What usually happens just before you slip back into the old pattern?
If a week has been chaotic, write a quick timeline of it. Order on paper can make a messy stretch feel more manageable.
Write a page about what you are proud of this month, however small. It is easy to forget good work once it is done.
Try journaling on the move today: a few lines on your phone in a queue or on a train. Habits survive best when they travel.
Write down a belief about yourself that you would like to test. Then note one small piece of evidence for and against it.
If you share a home, find a quiet corner or a regular slot that is yours for writing, even ten minutes. Protect it gently.
When the day has been dull and there seems nothing to say, write about that. Boredom has its own useful information.
Two months of pages. Write down what writing gives you that nothing else quite does. Keep that note somewhere easy to reread.
Try a weekly review: on one evening, read back the past seven entries and write three lines on patterns you notice.
Write about a choice you made well recently. What did you know, or do, that helped you make it?
When you are angry, write the furious version first and do not hold back on the page. Then write the calmer version you might actually say.
Write about a skill you are slowly getting better at. Recording progress makes the slow middle stretch easier to bear.
Try a monthly page at the front or back of your notebook listing the main themes you wrote about. It becomes a map of your thinking.
Write about someone you admire whom you know personally. What do they do that you would like to borrow?
If writing has started to feel like a chore, change one thing: a new pen, a new spot, or a shorter entry. Small novelty helps.
Write down something you have been avoiding thinking about. You do not need to solve it today, only name it on the page.
Try writing in the third person today, about yourself. It can create just enough distance to see a situation more fairly.
When plans fall apart, write what you can still control and what you cannot. Then put your energy into the first column.
Write about a time you changed your mind about something important. What finally tipped it?
Notice whether you write more honestly when you know nobody will read it. Keep your notebook private if that helps you speak freely.
Write a page about a relationship that has shifted lately. Avoid blame, and simply describe what is different now.
Ten weeks in. If someone asked whether you are a person who journals, what would you honestly say? Write your answer down.
Write about how your pages have helped you this season, with one concrete example of something you understood better.
Try rereading an entry from a difficult day. Write a kind line in the margin, as you might for a friend.
Write down what a good-enough entry looks like for you. Having a minimum makes it easier to keep going on tired days.
If you are travelling or your routine is disrupted, decide in advance what the smallest version of your habit will be.
Write about something you used to worry about that no longer troubles you. Your old pages may hold the proof.
Try collecting good questions on one page as you come across them. On a stuck day, pick one and write.
Write about what you want the next three months to feel like, not just what you want to achieve.
Notice when you reach for your notebook without being reminded. That instinct is the habit becoming part of you.
Write about how you would explain your journaling habit to someone who thinks it sounds self-indulgent.
Choose a shelf or box for your finished notebooks. Keeping them together turns scattered pages into a record of your thinking.
Write down the few rules that make your habit work: when, where, how long, and what to do on a missed day.
When the next big change comes, plan to write through it. Pages are especially useful when life is in motion.
Write about who you were at the start of these ninety days, and who sits here writing now. Be specific and generous.
Nearly there. Read through your favourite entries and copy two or three lines onto a fresh page as a reminder for later.
Write a short note to yourself to open in a year: what you hope your pages will still be helping you with by then.
That brings these ninety days to a close. Keep the notebook close, keep the entries short when you need to, and let writing remain a quiet place to think.
